name: Giant cell tumour of tendon sheath

clinicalPearls: The second commonest soft-tissue tumour of the hand after the ganglion, presenting as a firm, slow-growing, painless nodule usually on the volar or lateral aspect of a digit.
It represents the localised form of tenosynovial giant cell tumour and is the small-joint counterpart of pigmented villonodular synovitis affecting large joints.
The mass is typically firm and does not transilluminate, which helps distinguish it clinically from a ganglion.
Lesions are commonest on the radial three digits and frequently overlie or abut the flexor tendon sheath and interphalangeal joints.
Longstanding tumours may cause pressure erosion of adjacent bone visible on plain radiographs, though frank bony invasion is unusual.
MRI shows characteristic low signal on T1 and T2 sequences with blooming artefact on gradient-echo imaging due to haemosiderin, aiding preoperative planning.
Treatment is marginal excision with removal of satellite nodules; incomplete excision is the main driver of the appreciable local recurrence rate.
Recurrence is more likely with lesions at the distal interphalangeal joint, those with bony involvement and multilobulated tumours, so careful excision and follow-up are warranted.
reference.pathophysiology: Giant cell tumour of the tendon sheath is a benign proliferative lesion of the synovial lining of tendon sheaths, bursae and joints. It is now recognised as a neoplastic process in most cases, frequently driven by a translocation involving the CSF1 gene that leads to overexpression of colony-stimulating factor 1 and recruitment of CSF1-receptor-bearing macrophages (a landscape effect). Histologically it comprises mononuclear stromal cells, multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells, foamy macrophages and haemosiderin-laden cells within a collagenous stroma, forming a well-circumscribed, often lobulated mass adherent to the tendon sheath.
additionalDifferentials: Ganglion cyst of the digit or tendon sheath
Glomus tumour when subungual and painful
Synovial sarcoma or other soft-tissue sarcoma
additionalInvestigations: MRI demonstrating a low-signal mass with gradient-echo blooming from haemosiderin
Ultrasound showing a solid hypoechoic mass adjacent to the tendon sheath
Plain radiographs to detect pressure erosion of adjacent bone
Histopathological confirmation after excision remains the diagnostic standard
Immunohistochemistry (for example clusterin and CD68) in equivocal histology
Assessment of the mass for transillumination to distinguish from a ganglion
Documentation of the tumour's relationship to the flexor sheath and neurovascular bundle
redFlags: Rapid enlargement, pain or ill-defined infiltrative margins suggesting a sarcoma
Cortical destruction or aggressive bony invasion rather than smooth pressure erosion
Recurrent or multinodular disease extending beyond the tendon sheath
Neurovascular compromise of the digit from mass effect
reference.prognosis: Benign with an excellent prognosis after complete marginal excision, but local recurrence is well recognised, particularly with incompletely excised, multilobulated or distal interphalangeal joint lesions; malignant transformation is very rare.
pitfalls: Mistaking the firm nodule for a ganglion and under-treating it
Leaving satellite nodules or intra-articular extension, resulting in recurrence
Damaging the digital neurovascular bundle, which is often intimately related to the tumour, during excision
Omitting radiographs and missing bony erosion that alters the surgical plan
Failing to send tissue for histology, so an unexpected sarcoma is missed
references: WHO Classification of Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours
management: Excise the tumour completely with a marginal plane as the mainstay of treatment
Remove multilobulated tumour and satellite nodules meticulously, clearing the tendon sheath and joint to lower recurrence
Reserve systemic CSF1-receptor-directed therapy such as pexidartinib for diffuse or unresectable tenosynovial disease
Plan excision with MRI to define extent and tendon or joint involvement
Provide postoperative hand therapy to restore digital movement
Monitor for local recurrence, which is commoner with incompletely excised or distal interphalangeal lesions
Manage under hand and plastic surgery
